analysis.one_liner: Directs the FTC to treat 'shrinkflation' — shrinking a product without cutting its price — as illegal deception.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Federal Trade Commission to write rules, within 18 months, defining 'shrinkflation' — a manufacturer shrinking a product while keeping its price the same or higher — as an unfair or deceptive practice, and to prohibit it. The FTC and state attorneys general could then enforce the ban the way other consumer-protection rules are enforced. The bill also cites research attributing a share of recent inflation to corporate profits and shrinkflation. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyday shoppers, especially families buying packaged groceries and household goods. If the FTC rules took effect, companies would either have to cut prices when they cut package sizes, or clearly absorb the change instead of quietly charging more per ounce. State attorneys general could also sue on behalf of residents to recover damages and restitution.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Shoppers buying packaged groceries and household goods

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the FTC to promulgate regulations, within 18 months of enactment, prohibiting manufacturers from downsizing a consumer product without decreasing its price by a commensurate amount.

Violations would be treated as unfair or deceptive practices under the FTC Act, giving the Commission its full enforcement powers, and state attorneys general could sue in federal court to enjoin violations, obtain civil penalties, and recover damages or restitution for residents.

The bill's findings state that Federal Reserve research attributed 42 percent of 2020-2022 inflation to greater corporate profits, and that BLS data show roughly 10 percent of inflation in some consumer product categories is driven by shrinkflation.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food and household-product manufacturers, who would either have to reduce prices in step with any downsizing — shrinking their per-unit margins — or keep package sizes the same and absorb input costs. Compliance with new FTC rules and exposure to FTC actions and state attorney general lawsuits would add costs.

drawbacks.text: A flat prohibition on downsizing without commensurate price cuts may simply push companies to raise the sticker price in plain view instead of shrinking the package, which would show up directly in reported inflation without necessarily making consumers better off — the honest objection a supporter would have to acknowledge.

The bill's requirements are broad — the FTC must define 'commensurate' price reductions by regulation, and manufacturers would face compliance costs and litigation exposure from both FTC enforcement and parens patriae suits by state attorneys general.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit to shoppers is real but modest: shrinkflation affects a slice of consumer prices, not wages or housing, so the bill would not have moved overall inflation much on its own. The design is blunt — banning the practice rather than requiring clear disclosure — which risks companies openly raising prices instead, though it also gives the FTC flexibility to modify the definition by regulation. The main reason it never mattered, though, is that it never got a hearing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez introduced the Shrinkflation Prevention Act of 2024 in the House on March 26, 2024, joined by Rep. Chris Deluzio.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and three days later to its Subcommittee on Innovation, Data, and Commerce.
The bill attracted 18 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no further action was taken; it died in committee when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food and household-product manufacturers are better off, since the ban never took effect and they can continue sizing products down without commensurate price cuts. The House majority that declined to schedule committee action also avoided a vote on the measure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Packaged-goods makers; the bill died without a vote

for.name: Rep. Chris Deluzio
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only original cosponsor at introduction.

for.name: 18 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; no Republican cosponsored the bill.

against.name: Rep. Cathy McMorris Rodgers
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Her committee received the bill by referral on March 26, 2024 and never scheduled a markup or floor action; the complete action history shows no further committee or floor activity.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: The bill received no Republican cosponsors and was never brought to the floor in the 118th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters — the sponsor and 18 cosponsors — were Democrats, and with the House under Republican control the bill never advanced out of committee or received a Republican cosponsor.

industries.industry: Packaged food and consumer goods manufacturers
industries.note: The bill would have forced these companies to cut prices proportionally when they shrink a product — or drop the practice — ending a quiet way to raise per-unit prices. The bill's own findings cite research showing consumers notice price changes more than size changes, which is why the tactic works on shoppers.

industries.industry: State attorneys general and consumer-protection enforcers
industries.note: The bill would have expanded state AGs' authority to sue manufacturers in federal court for shrinkflation violations, with power to seek penalties, damages, and restitution for residents.
